newsitem.title: USA: Maverick tobacco CEO a puzzle to trial lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Maverick tobacco CEO a puzzle to trial lawyers.

text.p: Renegade tobacco executive Bennett LeBow will take the witness stand on Monday in a $5 billion secondhand-smoke trial, creating a puzzle for tobacco lawyers since his Liggett Group is a defendant in the case even while he is cooperating with anti-tobacco forces.
LeBow, a Florida resident, is the only chief executive of the five leading tobacco companies expected to testify before the six-person jury in the landmark secondhand-smoke trial.
Others, such as the head of Philip Morris Inc., had pretrial testimony presented on videotape or by readings of their answers in court.

Head of the parent of Liggett Group Inc., which makes Chesterfield, Lark and other brands, LeBow was subpoenaed by the lawyers pressing the suit, which claims that respiratory and other illnesses suffered by 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants were caused by cigarette smoke aboard U.S. airliners.
The lawyers, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, declined to detail the questions they will put to LeBow.
But consultants and others attending the trial said the lawyers are sure to question the executive about his turnaround on smoking's health risks.

LeBow last spring became the first tobacco executive to acknowledge in public that decades of medical research were conclusive and that smoking was dangerous and that nicotine, a component of cigarettes, was addictive.

Battling to keep Liggett from bankruptcy, LeBow cut a deal with state officials suing the tobacco industry to effectively turn state's evidence against his peers and hand over industry documents that experts said hurt Big Tobacco's legal defence.

He also promised in an agreement earlier this year to put stern warning labels on Chesterfield and other Liggett brands, in a deal that helped spur the $368 billion settlement between tobacco companies and state officials announced in June.
LeBow has denounced the national settlement, saying its terms would destroy Liggett, the smallest of the major tobacco companies with only 2 percent of the U.S. cigarette market.

It was unclear whether lawyers for Liggett would question LeBow but consultants said one of the dozen or more lawyers defending the tobacco companies and industry groups in the trial was sure to cross examine the executive.
"A lawyer from Reynolds or whomever will cross examine LeBow," one trial consultant said. "That'll be unusual, with Liggett's lawyers sitting beside them."

During last week's opening arguments, a Liggett lawyer pointedly separated his company's practices and history from Philip Morris and other others. "Liggett is different," attorney Michael Fay told the jurors.

The Rosenblatts last week presented three expert witnesses, including a retired U.S. Surgeon General, who testified that secondhand smoke caused lung cancer and other diseases and that flight attendants encountered more smoke than bartenders.
Tobacco company lawyers say the secondhand smoke on airplanes before a 1988 ban on smoking did not constitute a health risk to anyone.
The trial is the first to test secondhand-smoke claims and is the first class-action suit against the U.S. cigarette makers. AMB.N
